subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: In this unit you will look more closely at solid shapes. You will name the cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone and pyramid, explain that a 3D shape takes up space, count the flat faces on a cube and a cuboid, find the curved surfaces, and sort shapes by whether they roll or stack.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 1 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Name common 3D shapes: cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone and pyramid.
Explain that a 3D shape is solid and takes up space, and that a 2D shape is flat.
Point to and count the flat faces on a cube and a cuboid.
Describe a curved surface and say which shapes have one.
Sort shapes into groups such as rolls / does not roll and stacks / does not stack.
Match a 3D shape to an everyday object of the same shape.
Say what is the same and what is different between two shapes.
Make and continue a simple pattern using 3D shapes.
A cube: a dice, a stock cube, or a small square building block.

concepts.title: Solid (3D) shapes take up space
concepts.explanation: Start with the big idea: 3D shapes are solid and take up space, while 2D shapes are flat. You do not need the words ‘dimension’ or ‘depth’ — you need to feel the difference. Put a flat paper circle on the table next to a real orange. Hold both. The paper is flat and floppy; the orange is solid and round, and you can turn it in your hand. How to teach it: Gather four or five solid objects from around the home — a tin, a date box, a ball, a dice. Pick each one up, turn it over, and feel that it is solid. Say each time, ‘This is a 3D shape. It takes up space. We can hold it.’ Then hold up a picture or a flat cut-out and say, ‘This is flat. It is a 2D shape.’ Sorting solid things from flat things is the whole lesson at this stage. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Hold the orange. Can you feel that it is solid all the way round?” Child: “Yes, it is round and hard.” You: “That makes it a 3D shape — it takes up space. Now feel this flat paper circle. Flat shapes are 2D.”
concepts.example: Play a quick sorting game across the week: put a pile of objects and a few flat paper shapes on the mat and make two groups — solid (3D) things you can hold, and flat (2D) shapes. Keep it playful and hands-on. The aim is that you can feel, not just say, the difference between a flat shape and a solid one.

concepts.title: Cubes and cuboids — faces and edges
concepts.explanation: A cube is a solid with 6 flat faces, and every face is a square the same size — think of a dice or a small building block. A cuboid also has 6 flat faces, but they are rectangles, so it looks like a stretched box — think of a date box, a matchbox, or a book. Both the cube and the cuboid have flat faces and straight edges, which is why they stack so well into towers. How to teach it: Give the child a dice (cube) and a date box (cuboid). Help them touch and count the faces — press one finger on each flat side, turning the shape, and count together, ‘one, two, three, four, five, six.’ Both have 6 faces. Then run a finger along an edge, the line where two faces meet, and say the word ‘edge’. Do not push the child to count all 12 edges — simply noticing that edges are the lines where faces meet is plenty at this age. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Let us count the flat faces on the dice. Touch each one as we turn it.” You and child: “One… two… three… four… five… six.” You: “Six faces! And they are all squares. That makes it a cube.” You: “Now the date box — count its faces too. Six again! But these are rectangles, so it is a cuboid.”
concepts.example: Bring out that a cube and a cuboid are the same in some ways and different in others. They are the same because both have 6 flat faces, straight edges and corners, and both can stack. They are different because a cube's faces are all equal squares, while a cuboid's faces are longer rectangles. Learning to say ‘what is the same and what is different’ is a key thinking skill in this unit, so model those exact words often.

concepts.title: Spheres and cylinders — curved surfaces
concepts.explanation: A sphere is round all over, like a ball or an orange. It has one curved surface, no flat faces, and no edges — nothing flat to rest on — so it rolls in every direction. A cylinder is like a tin of tomatoes: it has two flat round ends (both circles, the same size) joined by one curved surface around the side. Because it has flat ends, a cylinder can stand and stack on its ends, but because its side is curved, it will also roll when it is on its side. How to teach it: Hand the child an orange and a tin. Run their finger over the orange — smooth and curved everywhere, no flat spots. Then over the tin — flat circle on top, flat circle on the bottom, but curved round the middle. Give the shapes a gentle push on the table so you see the orange roll away easily and the tin roll only when it is lying on its side. This is the heart of the ‘rolls / does not roll’ idea in Concept 5. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Feel the orange. Can you find any flat part?” Child: “No, it is round everywhere.” You: “That curved surface is why it rolls. Now feel the tin — flat top, flat bottom, curved side.” You: “Stand the tin up. It balances on its flat end! Lay it down and push — now it rolls.”
concepts.example: A common and useful comparison is sphere versus cylinder: what is the same, what is different? Both have a curved surface and both can roll. But a sphere has no flat faces, so it can never stand still on a table, while a cylinder has two flat circle faces, so it can stand up on one end. Handling the two objects side by side makes this clear far better than any picture.

concepts.title: Cones and pyramids — shapes with a point
concepts.explanation: A cone has one flat round face at the bottom and a curved surface that rises to a single point at the top — think of a party hat or an ice-cream cone. A pyramid has a flat base (often a square or a triangle) and flat triangle faces that lean in and meet at a point at the top — think of the great pyramids or a tent. Both shapes come to a point, which children love, and both can sit still on their flat bottom. How to teach it: A cone is easy to make — roll a semicircle of paper into a party-hat shape and tape it. Feel the point at the top and the round opening at the bottom. If you have a pyramid (or fold one from card), count its flat triangle faces and find the point where they meet. Keep this concept light: naming the cone and pyramid and noticing their point is the goal, not counting every face.
concepts.example: You can gently explore that a cone is a little like a cylinder that has been squeezed to a point, and a pyramid is a little like a cuboid that has been squeezed to a point. This is just playful talk, not a rule to memorise — but it helps you see how the solid shapes relate to one another.

concepts.title: Sorting — rolls, stacks and everyday objects
concepts.explanation: This is where the unit comes together. Once you can name the shapes, you should sort them by what they do. Two sorts work beautifully for this age. First, rolls / does not roll: spheres and cylinders and cones have curved surfaces, so they roll; cubes and cuboids have only flat faces, so they do not. Second, stacks / does not stack: shapes with flat faces (cube, cuboid, and a cylinder on its flat end) can be built into a tower, while a sphere cannot balance and will roll away. How to teach it: Draw two big circles or lay two hoops or plates on the floor and label them (say them aloud for the child) ‘rolls’ and ‘does not roll’. Give the child the basket of shapes and test each one with a gentle push before dropping it into the right group. Then do the same for ‘stacks’ and ‘tips over’ by trying to build a little tower. Testing and sorting real objects is far more powerful than any worksheet. Finish by linking every shape back to everyday objects, because this is what makes geometry stick. Walk around the home together on a ‘shape hunt’: the tin and the cup are cylinders, the orange and the football are spheres, the date box and the book are cuboids, the dice is a cube, the party hat is a cone. When you can point around the room and name the solid shapes, the unit has done its work. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Push each shape gently. Does it roll, or stay still?” You: “The ball rolls — it goes in the rolls group. The date box stays still — it goes in the other group.” You: “Now let us go on a shape hunt. Can you find something in our home shaped like a tin? That is a cylinder!” Confusing 2D and 3D. You call a solid cube a ‘square’ or a ball a ‘circle’. Keep a flat paper shape next to the solid object and stress: flat is 2D, solid you can hold is 3D. Thinking bigger means a different shape. A small dice and a big box can both be cubes/cuboids — and two cylinders of different sizes are both cylinders. Size does not change the shape name. Show shapes of different sizes side by side.
concepts.example: Miscounting faces. You count the same face twice or misses one. Slow them down: turn the shape and touch each face once, moving in a steady order.

explorations.title: Solid (3D) shapes take up space
explorations.context: Start with the big idea: 3D shapes are solid and take up space, while 2D shapes are flat. You do not need the words ‘dimension’ or ‘depth’ — you need to feel the difference. Put a flat paper circle on the table next to a real orange.
explorations.prompt: Hold a real orange and a flat paper circle. Which one is the 3D shape, and how can you tell?
explorations.answer: The orange — it is solid and takes up space. The paper circle is flat, so it is a 2D shape.
explorations.hint: Turn each one in your hand — does it stay round and solid all over, or is it flat and thin?
explorations.explanation: The orange stays solid and round no matter how you turn it, while the paper circle is only a thin, flat outline — that felt difference is exactly what makes something 3D rather than 2D. Once you can sort a handful of household objects the same way, you have the one idea the rest of this unit is built on: a 3D shape is solid and takes up space, and a 2D shape is flat.

explorations.title: Cubes and cuboids — faces and edges
explorations.context: A cube is a solid with 6 flat faces, and every face is a square the same size — think of a dice or a small building block.
explorations.prompt: Count the flat faces on a dice as you turn it. How many faces does a dice (a cube) have?
explorations.hint: Touch one face at a time and turn the dice, counting aloud as you go.
explorations.explanation: A cube's six faces are all equal squares, which is why a dice looks the same from every side, while a cuboid's six faces are rectangles, so it looks longer in one direction, like a date box. Because both shapes have only flat faces meeting at straight edges, they sit still and stack neatly — counting the faces together makes this real instead of just naming the two shapes.

explorations.title: Spheres and cylinders — curved surfaces
explorations.context: A sphere is round all over, like a ball or an orange. It has one curved surface, no flat faces, and no edges — nothing flat to rest on — so it rolls in every direction.
explorations.prompt: Run your finger all the way around a ball. Can you find any flat part on it?
explorations.answer: No — a ball (sphere) has no flat part; it is curved all over, which is why it rolls.
explorations.hint: Try to find a straight, flat spot anywhere on the ball's surface.
explorations.explanation: A sphere has no flat part anywhere, so it rolls whichever way it is nudged, while a cylinder's two flat round ends let it stand and stack even though its curved side still lets it roll when lying on its side. Noticing which parts of each shape are flat and which are curved explains why these two solids behave so differently once you push them.

explorations.title: Cones and pyramids — shapes with a point
explorations.context: A cone has one flat round face at the bottom and a curved surface that rises to a single point at the top — think of a party hat or an ice-cream cone.
explorations.prompt: Look at a party hat. What 3D shape is it?
explorations.hint: Think of a shape with one flat round bottom and a curved surface that rises to a point.
explorations.explanation: Both shapes narrow to a single point, but a cone gets there through one curved surface while a pyramid gets there through several flat triangular faces meeting at the top — that is the real difference between them, not just their overall outline. Because each also has a flat base, both can stand still on a table, which is why a party hat and a toy pyramid both balance rather than roll away.

explorations.title: Sorting — rolls, stacks and everyday objects
explorations.context: This is where the unit comes together. Once you can name the shapes, you should sort them by what they do. Two sorts work beautifully for this age.
explorations.prompt: Will a ball roll away if you give it a gentle push?
explorations.answer: Yes, it rolls, because it has a curved surface touching the table all the way round.
explorations.hint: Check whether any flat part of the ball is touching the table.
explorations.explanation: Shapes with a curved surface touching the table — a ball, a cylinder or a cone lying on its side — roll, while shapes resting on a flat face — a cube, a cuboid, or a cylinder or cone standing on its flat end — can stack; testing this by gently pushing each object and then trying to build a tower turns the sorting rule into something you can see for themselves. Matching each shape to a real object from around the home, like a tin or a ball, is what makes the shape names stick beyond this one lesson.

explorations.title: You can gently explore that a cone
explorations.context: You can gently explore that a cone is a little like a cylinder that has been squeezed to a point, and a pyramid is a little like a cuboid that has been squeezed to a point.
explorations.prompt: A cone is like a cylinder squeezed to a point. Using that same idea, what shape does a cuboid become when it is squeezed to a point?
explorations.hint: Think of the shape with flat triangle faces that lean in and meet at a point, like a tent.
explorations.explanation: Thinking of a cone as a cylinder squeezed to a point, and a pyramid as a cuboid squeezed to a point, gives you a playful way to connect the round shapes to the pointed shapes instead of treating all six shapes as separate, unrelated facts. It is not a rule to be tested on — it is a way to help the shapes feel like one connected family.

methods.title: Naming 3D shapes from real objects
methods.example: Hold up a stock cube, a can of beans, a football and a party hat, one at a time, and name each shape.
steps: Gather one real example of each shape: a cube (dice), a cuboid (matchbox), a sphere (ball), a cylinder (tin), a cone (party hat) and a pyramid (toy or picture).
Hold up one object at a time and say its shape name together, e.g. 'This is a cylinder.'
Mix the objects up and take turns picking one up and naming it without help.

methods.title: Solid versus flat: sorting real vs paper shapes
methods.example: Compare a real orange (solid, 3D) with a paper circle cut from card (flat, 2D).
steps: Place a solid object (an orange) and a flat paper shape (a paper circle) side by side on the table.
Pick each one up and describe what they feel: 'round and hard all over' versus 'flat and thin'.
Say together: 'The orange is a 3D shape because it takes up space. The paper circle is a 2D shape because it is flat.'

methods.title: Counting the faces of a cube and a cuboid
methods.example: Touch and count each flat face of a dice (cube) and a cereal box (cuboid).
steps: Give the child a dice and ask them to press one finger on a flat face and say 'one face'.
Turn the dice to a new face each time and count aloud together up to six.
Repeat with a cuboid (cereal box), counting its six rectangular faces the same way.

methods.title: Finding the curved surface on a ball and a tin
methods.example: Run a finger around a football and a tin of tomatoes to feel where the surface curves.
steps: Hand the child a ball and ask them to run a finger all the way around it without stopping.
Ask: 'Can you find any flat, straight part?' — they should find none; the whole surface curves.
Repeat with a tin, showing that it has a curved surface around the side but flat circles at the top and bottom.

methods.title: Sorting shapes into rolls and stacks
methods.example: Test a ball, a tin, and a box on a gentle slope to see which ones roll.
steps: Draw or lay out two hoops or sheets of paper labelled 'Rolls' and 'Does not roll'.
Gently push each object (ball, tin, dice, box) and watch which ones roll away and which stay still.
Sort the same objects again into 'Stacks' and 'Does not stack' by trying to build a small tower with each.

methods.title: Matching shapes to household objects
methods.example: Match a dice to a cube, a can to a cylinder, and a ball to a sphere.
steps: Lay out shape name cards or say the shape names: cube, cylinder, sphere, cone, cuboid, pyramid.
Walk around the home together and find one real object for each shape name.
Place each object next to its matching shape name and say the sentence: 'This can is a cylinder.'

workedExamples.title: Naming three shapes at home
workedExamples.prompt: Amina finds a ball, a party hat, and a matchbox on the table. Help her name each 3D shape.
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Look at the ball — it is round all over with no flat parts, so it is a sphere. Step 2: Look at the party hat — it has one point at the top and a curved side, so it is a cone. Step 3: Look at the matchbox — it has 6 flat rectangular faces, so it is a cuboid. Amina says: 'ball = sphere, party hat = cone, matchbox = cuboid.'

workedExamples.title: Is it solid or flat?
workedExamples.prompt: Hassan holds a wooden block and a paper square cut from card. Which one is the 3D shape and which is the 2D shape?
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Pick up the wooden block — it is solid all the way through and takes up space, so it is a 3D shape. Step 2: Pick up the paper square — it is thin and flat with no thickness you can feel, so it is a 2D shape. Step 3: Say together: 'The block is 3D because it is solid; the paper square is 2D because it is flat.'

workedExamples.title: Counting the faces of a stock cube
workedExamples.prompt: Fatima holds a stock cube box. How many flat faces does it have?
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Turn the stock cube box so one flat side faces up and press a finger on it — that is 1 face. Step 2: Turn it over and press a finger on each new flat side, counting aloud: two, three, four, five, six. Step 3: There are no more sides to turn to, so the stock cube (a cube) has 6 flat faces.

workedExamples.title: Which shapes have a curved surface?
workedExamples.prompt: Look at a football, a tin of tomatoes, and a dice. Which ones have a curved surface?
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Run a finger over the football — it curves all the way round with no flat part, so it has a curved surface. Step 2: Run a finger around the side of the tin — the side curves, so it also has a curved surface (though its top and bottom are flat circles). Step 3: Run a finger over the dice — every side is flat, so the dice has no curved surface at all.

workedExamples.title: Sorting objects into rolls and stacks
workedExamples.prompt: Yusuf has a ball, a tin, and a box. Which objects roll, and which ones can be stacked?
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Gently push the ball — it rolls away because it is round all over (a sphere). Step 2: Gently push the tin on its side — it rolls too, because its curved side touches the table. Step 3: Try to stack the box on top of the tin standing upright — the box stacks because it has flat faces, but the ball cannot be stacked because it has no flat part to rest on.

workedExamples.title: Matching a dice and a football to their shapes
workedExamples.prompt: 🎲 → ____________  ⚽ → ____________ . Write the 3D shape name for each object.
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Look at the dice (🎲) — it has 6 flat square faces, so it matches the shape cube. Step 2: Look at the football (⚽) — it is round all over with no flat faces, so it matches the shape sphere. Step 3: Complete the sentences: 'A dice → cube. A football → sphere.'

workedExamples.title: Matching a tin and a box to their shapes
workedExamples.prompt: 🥫 → ____________  📦 → ____________ . Write the 3D shape name for each object.
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Look at the tin (🥫) — it has two flat round ends and a curved side, so it matches the shape cylinder. Step 2: Look at the box (📦) — it has 6 flat rectangular faces, so it matches the shape cuboid. Step 3: Complete the sentences: 'A tin → cylinder. A box → cuboid.'

workedExamples.title: Deciding if a cone rolls or stacks
workedExamples.prompt: Layla has a party hat shaped like a cone. Will it roll, will it stack, or both?
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Lay the cone on its curved side — it rolls in a circle because of its curved surface. Step 2: Stand the cone on its flat round bottom — it can sit still and even hold one small block on top, so it can stack a little on its flat base. Step 3: The answer is: a cone can roll (on its side) and can also stack (when it stands on its flat base).

workedExamples.title: Writing ROLL or STACK for four shapes
workedExamples.prompt: Look at a ball, a cube, a cylinder lying on its side, and a cone standing up. Write ROLL or STACK for each one.
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: The ball (sphere) has a curved surface all over and no flat part, so it is ROLL. Step 2: The cube has 6 flat faces and straight edges, so it is STACK. Step 3: The cylinder lying on its side has a curved surface touching the table, so it is ROLL. Step 4: The cone standing on its flat round base can hold things on top, so it is STACK.

workedExamples.title: Naming the shape of a ball
workedExamples.prompt: A ball → ____________ . Write the correct 3D shape name.
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Look at the ball — it is round all over with one curved surface and no flat faces or edges. Step 2: A shape that is round all over is called a sphere. Step 3: Complete the sentence: 'A ball → sphere.'

workedExamples.title: Naming the shape of a box
workedExamples.prompt: A box → ____________ . Write the correct 3D shape name.
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Look at the box — it has 6 flat faces, and they are rectangles rather than squares. Step 2: A solid with 6 flat rectangular faces is called a cuboid. Step 3: Complete the sentence: 'A box → cuboid.'

workedExamples.title: Naming the shape of a dice
workedExamples.prompt: A dice → ____________ . Write the correct 3D shape name.
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Look at the dice — it has 6 flat faces, and every face is a square the same size. Step 2: A solid with 6 equal square faces is called a cube. Step 3: Complete the sentence: 'A dice → cube.'

practice.prompt: Look at a football. Is it a 3D shape or a 2D shape? Explain how you know.
practice.answer: It is a 3D shape (a sphere) because it is solid, round all over, and takes up space — you can hold it in your hands.
practice.hint: Feel the ball all over — can you find any flat part?

practice.prompt: Point to a stock cube. How many flat faces can you count?
practice.answer: 6 flat faces — a stock cube is a cube, and every cube has 6 square faces.
practice.hint: Turn the stock cube slowly and touch each new flat side as you count.

practice.prompt: Hold a tin of beans and a dice. Which one has a curved surface?
practice.answer: The tin has a curved surface around its side, joining its two flat round ends. The dice has no curved surface — every side is flat.
practice.hint: Run your finger around the side of each object.

practice.prompt: Name this shape: it has one flat round face and a curved surface that rises to a point, like a party hat.
practice.hint: Think of an ice-cream cone or a party hat.

practice.prompt: Sort these into 'rolls' and 'stacks': a ball, a cereal box, a tin lying on its side.
practice.answer: Rolls: the ball and the tin lying on its side (both have a curved surface touching the table). Stacks: the cereal box (it has flat faces so it can be built into a tower).
practice.hint: Try to gently push each object — the ones that move away easily roll.

practice.prompt: 🎲 → ____________  ⚽ → ____________ . Write the shape name for the dice and the football.
practice.hint: The dice has flat square faces; the football is round all over.

practice.prompt: 🥫 → ____________  📦 → ____________ . Write the shape name for the tin and the box.
practice.hint: The tin has flat round ends and a curved side; the box has flat rectangular faces.

practice.prompt: Will a party hat (cone) roll, stack, or both? Explain your answer.
practice.answer: Both — a cone rolls when it lies on its curved side, and it can stack (sit still and hold something small) when it stands on its flat round base.
practice.hint: Try laying the cone on its side, then try standing it up on its flat end.

practice.prompt: Write ROLL or STACK for each: a ball, a matchbox, a party hat lying on its side.
practice.answer: Ball → ROLL. Matchbox → STACK. Party hat lying on its side → ROLL.
practice.hint: Curved surface touching the table means ROLL; flat faces touching the table mean STACK.

practice.prompt: A ball → ____________ . Write the 3D shape name.
practice.hint: Round all over, with one curved surface.

practice.prompt: A box → ____________ . Write the 3D shape name.
A dice → ____________ . Write the 3D shape name.
practice.hint: 6 flat square faces, all the same size.

activities.title: Practise together
activities.materials: Paper, pencil and familiar household objects
steps: Choose one idea from this unit.
Build or draw a model of it.
Explain your model to a family member.
Write one question of your own and solve it.

rules.title: Cones and Pyramids Are Like Squeezed Shapes
rules.text: You can gently explore that a cone is a little like a cylinder that has been squeezed to a point, and a pyramid is a little like a cuboid that has been squeezed to a point. This is just playful talk, not a rule to memorise — but it helps you see how the solid shapes relate to one another.

terms: A solid shape that takes up space; you can hold it
A flat shape, like a shape drawn on paper
A flat surface on a 3D shape
The line where two faces meet
To move by turning over and over
To build up, one on top of another
Round all over, one curved surface
2 round flat ends, curved in between
A round flat bottom rising to a point
commonMistakes: A common mistake is calling it a 'circle'
Remember that a circle is a flat shape drawn on paper, while the football is solid — the correct 3D name is sphere.
A common mistake is saying the tins 'roll' when stacked upright
Remember that on their flat ends the tins stand still and stack; they would only roll if placed on their curved side.
A common mistake is stopping the count at 4, forgetting the top and bottom faces
Remember to turn the lunch box over and count the top and the bottom too.
A common mistake is calling the printed picture '3D' because it shows a teapot shape
Remember that a picture of an object is still flat and 2D, even if the object it shows is solid.
A common mistake is saying the can of oil never rolls
Remember that whether the can rolls depends on how it is resting — on its curved side it rolls, but on its flat end it stands still.

fluency.prompt: Hold a football in your hand. What 3D shape is it?
fluency.hint: It is round all over, with no flat parts.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you say 'circle', remember a circle is flat (2D) and drawn on paper, but a football is solid and round all over — that makes it a sphere.

fluency.prompt: Hold a matchbox. Is it a cube or a cuboid?
fluency.answer: A cuboid, because its faces are rectangles, not squares.
fluency.hint: Check whether every face is the same size and shape.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you say 'cube', have them compare the long and short sides of the matchbox — a cube's faces must all be equal squares, but a matchbox's faces are rectangles, so it is a cuboid.

fluency.prompt: Hold a tin and a dice. Which shape can roll on its side?
fluency.answer: The tin (a cylinder) can roll on its side.
fluency.hint: Look for a curved surface that can touch the table.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you say the dice can roll, remember the dice has only flat faces, so it slides or tips over but does not roll like the curved side of the tin.

fluency.prompt: Name a shape that has a curved surface and one point at the top.
fluency.hint: Think of a party hat or an ice-cream cone.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you say 'pyramid', remember a pyramid comes to a point using flat triangle faces, while a cone's side is one curved surface, not flat triangles.

fluency.prompt: Would a cereal box roll away if you gave it a gentle push?
fluency.answer: No — a cereal box (a cuboid) has only flat faces, so it does not roll; it may slide or tip over instead.
fluency.hint: Check whether the box has any curved part touching the table.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you say 'yes, it rolls', have them push it gently and watch — it slides or falls over rather than turning over and over like a ball.

fluency.hint: One has flat square faces; the other is round all over.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you swap the answers, have them count the dice's flat faces (6, so cube) and check the football has none (so sphere).

fluency.hint: One has flat round ends and a curved side; the other has flat rectangular faces.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you call the tin a 'circle', remember a circle is flat and drawn on paper, but the tin is solid with a curved side and two flat round ends — that makes it a cylinder.

fluency.prompt: Can a party hat (cone) stack another small block on top of it?
fluency.answer: No — a cone comes to a point at the top, so nothing can balance there; it can only stand still on its flat base.
fluency.hint: Look at the very top of the cone — is it flat or pointed?
fluency.errorFeedback: If you say 'yes', ask them to try balancing a block on the pointed tip — it will fall off, because only flat surfaces can hold a stack.

fluency.prompt: Write ROLL or STACK: a football, a stock cube box, a can lying on its side.
fluency.answer: Football → ROLL. Stock cube box → STACK. Can lying on its side → ROLL.
fluency.hint: Curved surface touching the table means ROLL; flat faces touching the table mean STACK.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you mark the stock cube box as ROLL, remember every face of a cube is flat, so it cannot turn over and over — it stacks instead.

fluency.prompt: A ball → ____________ . Write the shape name.
fluency.hint: Round all over, one curved surface, no flat faces.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you write 'circle', remember a circle is a flat 2D shape, while a ball is solid and 3D — the solid round shape is called a sphere.

fluency.prompt: A box → ____________ . Write the shape name.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you write 'cube', have them check if all the faces are equal squares — a box with rectangle faces is a cuboid, not a cube.

fluency.prompt: A dice → ____________ . Write the shape name.
fluency.hint: 6 flat square faces, all the same size.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you write 'cuboid', have them check that every face of the dice is an equal square — that makes it specifically a cube, a special kind of cuboid.

realProblems.prompt: At home, Amina picks up a football from under the bed. What 3D shape is the football, and how does she know?
realProblems.answer: The football is a sphere, because it is round all over with one curved surface and no flat faces.
realProblems.hint: Have her run her hand all over the ball to check for any flat spot.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is calling it a 'circle'. Remember that a circle is a flat shape drawn on paper, while the football is solid — the correct 3D name is sphere.

realProblems.prompt: At the market, Hassan sees a stack of tinned tomatoes. What shape is each tin, and why can they be stacked?
realProblems.answer: Each tin is a cylinder. They can be stacked because each tin has two flat round ends, so one tin can sit flat on top of another.
realProblems.hint: Look at the top and bottom of the tin — are they flat or curved?
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying the tins 'roll' when stacked upright. Remember that on their flat ends the tins stand still and stack; they would only roll if placed on their curved side.

realProblems.prompt: On the bus, Fatima notices her water bottle cap looks like a tiny cylinder, and her lunch box is shaped like a cuboid. How many flat faces does the lunch box have?
realProblems.answer: 6 flat faces, because a cuboid (like a rectangular lunch box) always has 6 flat rectangular faces.
realProblems.hint: Have her touch and count each flat side of the lunch box, one at a time.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is stopping the count at 4, forgetting the top and bottom faces. Remember to turn the lunch box over and count the top and the bottom too.

realProblems.prompt: Every morning, Yusuf drinks his tea from a solid clay cup and looks at a flat picture of a teapot printed on the tablecloth. Which one is the 3D shape and which is the 2D shape?
realProblems.answer: The clay cup is a 3D shape because it is solid and takes up space — Yusuf can pick it up and turn it. The printed picture of the teapot is a 2D shape because it is flat, just ink on the cloth.
realProblems.hint: Ask: can you pick it up and turn it in your hand? If yes, it is 3D.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is calling the printed picture '3D' because it shows a teapot shape. Remember that a picture of an object is still flat and 2D, even if the object it shows is solid.

realProblems.prompt: At home, Layla helps sort the kitchen shelf: a box of dates (cuboid), a ball of dough, and a can of oil. Which of these three will roll if nudged?
realProblems.answer: The ball of dough will roll, because it is a sphere with a curved surface all over. The can of oil will roll only if it is lying on its side; standing upright it will not roll. The box of dates will not roll because it has only flat faces.
realProblems.hint: Think about which shapes have a curved surface touching the shelf.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying the can of oil never rolls. Remember that whether the can rolls depends on how it is resting — on its curved side it rolls, but on its flat end it stands still.

realProblems.prompt: Layla's grandmother gives her a party hat shaped like a cone for a celebration. Can Layla stand the hat upright on the table, and can she roll it?
realProblems.answer: Yes to both — Layla can stand the cone upright on its flat round base, and she can also make it roll by laying it on its curved side and giving it a push.
realProblems.hint: Try both: stand it on its flat end, then lay it on its side.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is thinking a shape can only roll OR only stack, never both. Remember that a cone can do both, depending on which part of it touches the table.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A tin of beans and a picture of a tin drawn on its label look similar. Explain why the tin itself is a 3D shape but the drawing on the label is a 2D shape.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The real tin is a 3D shape because it is solid, takes up space, and you can pick it up and turn it in your hands — it also has flat faces (the round top and bottom) and a curved surface around the side. The drawing on the label is a 2D shape because it is flat: it has no thickness you can feel, and it only shows what the tin looks like from one side.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why a cereal box (cuboid) can be stacked into a tower but a football (sphere) cannot.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The cereal box can be stacked because it has flat faces and straight edges — a flat face can rest evenly on another flat face without wobbling. The football cannot be stacked because it has one curved surface all over and no flat face anywhere, so anything placed on it, or the ball itself placed on something, will roll off.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A cylinder (like a tin) has both a flat part and a curved part. Explain what is flat, what is curved, and why the tin can both stand still and roll.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A tin's top and bottom are flat, round faces, and the side that goes around the middle is one curved surface. Because the top and bottom are flat, the tin can stand still and even stack when it rests on one of those ends. Because the side is curved, the tin will roll if it is lying on its side and given a push.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Cones and pyramids — shapes with a point.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A cone has one flat round face at the bottom and a curved surface that rises to a single point at the top — think of a party hat or an ice-cream cone. A pyramid has a flat base (often a square or a triangle) and flat triangle faces that lean in and meet at a point at the top — think of the great pyramids or a tent. Both shapes come to a point, which children love, and both can sit still on their flat bottom. How to teach it: A cone is easy to make — roll a semicircle of paper into a party-hat shape and tape it. Feel the point at the top and the round opening at the bottom. If you have a pyramid (or fold one from card), count its flat triangle faces and find the point where they meet. Keep this concept light: naming the cone and pyramid and noticing their point is the goal, not counting every face.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Sorting — rolls, stacks and everyday objects.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: This is where the unit comes together. Once you can name the shapes, you should sort them by what they do. Two sorts work beautifully for this age. First, rolls / does not roll: spheres and cylinders and cones have curved surfaces, so they roll; cubes and cuboids have only flat faces, so they do not. Second, stacks / does not stack: shapes with flat faces (cube, cuboid, and a cylinder on its flat end) can be built into a tower, while a sphere cannot balance and will roll away. How to teach it: Draw two big circles or lay two hoops or plates on the floor and label them (say them aloud for the child) ‘rolls’ and ‘does not roll’. Give the child the basket of shapes and test each one with a gentle push before dropping it into the right group. Then do the same for ‘stacks’ and ‘tips over’ by trying to build a little tower. Testing and sorting real objects is far more powerful than any worksheet.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why a cone is a little like a cylinder squeezed to a point, and a pyramid is a little like a cuboid squeezed to a point.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: You can gently explore that a cone is a little like a cylinder that has been squeezed to a point, and a pyramid is a little like a cuboid that has been squeezed to a point. This is just playful talk, not a rule to memorise — but it helps you see how the solid shapes relate to one another.

selfAssessment: I can name common 3D shapes: cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone and pyramid.
I can explain that a 3D shape is solid and takes up space, and that a 2D shape is flat.
I can point to and count the flat faces on a cube and a cuboid.
I can describe a curved surface and say which shapes have one.
I can sort shapes into groups such as rolls / does not roll and stacks / does not stack.
I can match a 3D shape to an everyday object of the same shape.
I can say what is the same and what is different between two shapes.
I can make and continue a simple pattern using 3D shapes.
